Case: A 49-year-old female with a history of Stiff Person Syndrome [on
biweekly Intravenous Immunoglobulin G (IVIG)], seizure disorder, type 1 diabetes mellitus, vitiligo,
pernicious anemia, history of chronic deep vein thrombosis, and sickle cell trait presented in the
context of being obtunded and was intubated for respiratory failure. Vitals were notable for
tachycardia of 129, afebrile, tachypnea of 36, and blood pressure of 143/80. Physical exam
revealed depigmented patches all over the body, coarse breath sounds bilaterally with rales
predominantly over right lung fields. Initial labs were notable for arterial pH 6.83, pCO2 39, pO2 190
mmHg, potassium 5.7 mmol/L, sodium 129 mmol/L, bicarbonate < 10 mmol, creatinine 1.32 mg/dL,
glucose 1,119 mg/dL, calcium 10.9 mg/dL, hyperproteinemia 9.6 gm/dL, lactic acid 8.2 mmol/L,
and leukocytosis 25,000 k/uL. Urinalysis was positive for glucosuria and ketones. The patient was
managed for Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA) with subsequent resolution in 2 days. Over the course of
hospitalization, chest imaging demonstrated the worsening of bilateral airspace opacities with the
progression of bilateral alveolar opacities, interlobular septal thickening, and ground-glass
attenuation throughout the lungs without intraluminal defects. The patient was maintained on low
tidal volume and high PEEP volume control settings with a target plateau pressure of < 30 cm of
water in the setting of ARDS. The patient was treated with methylprednisolone 40 mg IV q12 hr. On
days 10-14, the patient remained hemodynamically stable and was eventually extubated
successfully. Discussion: The patient was initially managed for DKA, however, given the rapidly
worsening respiratory failure, pulmonary evaluation became critical. Histology confirmed patterns of
diffuse alveolar damage. Interstitial lung diseases are challenging to diagnose with overlapping
presentations. They should be suspected in patients presenting with fulminant ARDS without a
history of underlying lung disease. Many case reports suggest managing interstitial pneumonia with
glucocorticoids and immunosuppression including rituximab. Our patient responded very well to
glucocorticoids and IVIG and was subsequently liberated from the ventilator after 14 days.
